summary: Describes an encoding that uses only printable ASCII characters to carry Chinese characters in email and network news messages. It exists because many mail systems of the time could not carry other byte values. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A code that spells out Chinese writing using only the keys on a basic keyboard.

questions: how to encode chinese in ascii email
why was hz encoding needed for chinese email
how to encode chinese text for ascii email
subtitle: Encoding Chinese text using only ASCII characters for email and network news

tldr.problem: Email and network news systems in the early 1990s were designed for ASCII only, making it difficult to transmit Chinese text which requires multiple bytes per character.
tldr.mechanism: HZ-GB-2312 encodes Chinese characters using printable ASCII character pairs, with escape sequences (~{ and ~}) to switch between ASCII and Chinese modes, keeping everything in the 7-bit ASCII range.
tldr.outcome: This encoding allowed Chinese text to pass through mail systems that were not 8-bit clean, and became widely supported across Chinese computing platforms on DOS, Mac, and Unix systems.

today: RFC 1842 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It documents an encoding that enabled Chinese text transmission when systems were ASCII-only, and it remains historically significant for demonstrating how character encoding problems were solved in the early internet.

sections.title: The Problem with Chinese on the Internet
sections.content:
Chinese and other East Asian languages use thousands of characters, which means each character needs more than one byte to represent. In the early 1990s, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), which carries email, was designed only for ASCII text (7-bit characters). Many mail systems could not handle 8-bit data reliably, corrupting any attempt to send Chinese text directly.

The RFC describes a practical solution: a 7-bit encoding method that had already been developed by Fung Fung Lee at Stanford and tested extensively on USENET newsgroups and internet forums over two years with considerable success.
sections.plainLanguage: Older email systems could only send plain English letters safely. Chinese needs more information per character, so people invented a clever trick to squeeze Chinese into the English format.

sections.title: How HZ-GB-2312 Works
sections.content:
The encoding uses two modes: ASCII mode and HZ mode. Text starts in ASCII mode, where regular characters are one byte each. To send Chinese, you write ~{ to enter HZ mode, then each Chinese character is represented as two printable ASCII characters (values 0x21-0x7E, the visible characters on a keyboard). To return to ASCII, you write ~}.

The tilde character ~ is special. In ASCII mode, ~~ represents a literal tilde. The sequence ~\n (tilde followed by newline) is used for line continuation. Other escape sequences like ~[!-z|] are reserved for future character sets.

Every line of text starts in ASCII mode by default, so Chinese text must be bracketed with mode-switch pairs on the same line or continued explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: It's like using two different codes. Normal mode is one character at a time. Chinese mode takes two characters at a time, and special marker combinations (like ~{ and ~}) switch between them.

sections.title: The Underlying Character Sets
sections.content:
HZ-GB-2312 represents Chinese characters from the GB 2312-80 standard, a coding scheme for the People's Republic of China that assigns two-byte codes to thousands of Chinese ideograms. In GB 2312, each character has a first byte in the range 0x21-0x77 and a second byte in the range 0x21-0x7E.

The key insight is that these byte ranges exactly match the printable ASCII range (0x21-0x7E). By using escape sequences to signal mode switches, two consecutive printable ASCII characters can safely carry one GB code point.

The RFC notes that future extensions could support additional GB character sets and other East Asian languages like Korean and Japanese.
sections.plainLanguage: Chinese character codes use the same number ranges as regular keyboard characters. So you can disguise a Chinese code as two keyboard characters, and markers tell the reader when to interpret them as Chinese instead of English.

sections.title: Formal Message Structure
sections.content:
Messages are structured as email headers followed by a body. The body consists of segments separated by single-byte-seq markers (~}), with each segment either entirely in ASCII or entirely in the Chinese character set (starting with ~{). A message must end in ASCII mode.

The formal grammar defines these as:

message = headers 1*( CRLF *single-byte-char *segment single-byte-seq *single-byte-char )

This ensures that parsers can cleanly identify what is Chinese and what is ASCII at every point in the transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages follow a pattern: header information, then a series of chunks. Each chunk is either pure English or pure Chinese, with markers between them.

sections.title: MIME Integration and Deployment
sections.content:
To use HZ-GB-2312 in email, senders specify Content-Type: text/plain; charset=HZ-GB-2312 in the MIME header. Since the encoding is already 7-bit, no Content-Transfer-Encoding header is needed; the text can be transmitted directly.

The RFC notes that HZ has been implemented in numerous software packages across DOS, Macintosh, and Unix platforms for tasks including word processing, file conversion, printing, terminal emulation, and communication. It was tested on USENET newsgroups alt.chinese.text and chinese.* for over two years, proving robust against corruption by diverse network systems and mail agents worldwide. This real-world testing on geographically scattered systems with vastly different environments gave confidence in its reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Email programs can declare a message is in HZ format, and any system that knows how to read it can decode the Chinese correctly. The fact that so many different programs support it, on so many different computers, proved it works reliably everywhere.
